solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Character of science magazine

definitions.meaning: a person's basic temperament or disposition
the long-running British weekly scientific journal of that name

explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: someone's inborn disposition, and the title of a leading weekly research journal.

clue.text: A relatively favourable employer?

parts.note: 'relatively' reads as 'fairly', but means 'towards relatives': a boss who favours family members

explanation.surface: A fairly kind boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'relatively' seems to mean 'comparatively' but really means 'to relatives'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who practises favouritism toward kin, especially in giving out jobs.

clue.text: Cat to mouse: no use escaping

indicators.note: escaping means these letters get away from the phrase before them

parts.note: taken as written; that the cat's letters open these words is a coincidence of the deletion, not a hidden word
O, a zero, means none

explanation.surface: A cat tells a mouse it is pointless trying to run away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'escaping' removes O (no) and USE from TO MOUSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A male feline, also the cat of the cartoon pair with Jerry.

clue.text: Charity event that is no fashion show!

definitions.text: Charity event that is no fashion show!

parts.words: Charity event that is no fashion show!
parts.note: students' fund-raising week in Britain; 'rag' also means a tatty garment, hence no catwalk

explanation.surface: A fund-raiser that is definitely not a catwalk event.
explanation.walkthrough: A RAG WEEK is a British university students' week of stunts raising money for charity; a rag is also shabby clothing, hence 'no fashion show'.
explanation.definitionFit: A students' week of fund-raising stunts for good causes, named with the word for tattered cloth.

clue.text: Small prehistoric circle within borders of certain area of Europe

parts.note: S is the usual abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

indicators.note: within means the circle sits inside the letters taken from the next word
the borders of a word are its first and last letters, here C and N

parts.note: a henge is a prehistoric circular earthwork or ring of stones, like Stonehenge

explanation.surface: A traveller notes a little stone circle near the edge of some region on the Continent.
explanation.definitionFit: The passport-free zone named after a Luxembourg village where the treaty was signed covers much of the continent.

clue.text: Carbon damage, very displeasing for PR campaign

parts.note: C is the chemical symbol for carbon
to harm is to damage
something offensive is highly displeasing

explanation.surface: A publicity drive damaged by carbon emissions proves very unpopular.
explanation.definitionFit: A concerted publicity drive to win people over with friendliness.

clue.text: No time for duck to catch seabird? It's endless

indicators.note: to catch means the letters close around the bird
no time means the time letter is removed

parts.note: a teal is a small duck
a tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: A duck has no time to catch a seabird; the chase is endless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No' takes the time letter from the duck, leaving EAL, and 'to catch' wraps that round the seabird.
explanation.definitionFit: Without end, everlasting, lasting for all time.

clue.text: Ransack Google — entire name missing, a pseudonym

indicators.note: to ransack is to turn things upside down, so the letters are jumbled
missing means a letter is left out of the words

explanation.surface: Search the web thoroughly, but a full name is missing; it must be an alias.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing' takes N from GOOGLE ENTIRE, and 'Ransack' rearranges the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The pen name of Mary Ann Evans, the Victorian novelist who wrote Middlemarch.

clue.text: Diarist's criticism of thin wine?

definitions.meaning: Charles Pooter, the diarist of the Grossmiths' comic novel, whose title calls him an insignificant person
a thin wine is said to lack fullness

explanation.surface: A diary writer complains about a weak wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The Diary of a Nobody is a comic English novel written as the diary of the clerk Charles Pooter.
explanation.definitionFit: The diarist is the nonentity of the Grossmiths' title, and a wine lacking fullness is said to lack body.

clue.text: A measure of traffic has to get through spreading green slime

parts.note: to pass is to get through, as through an exam

indicators.note: spreading means the letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A traffic statistic must cope with green slime spreading over the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A transport statistic: one traveller carried over one mile, used to quantify passenger traffic.

clue.text: In Australia, English stone said to be in fruit

indicators.note: said means the words are heard spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: Australians call an English person a Pommie, and granite is a hard stone

explanation.surface: Something about an Englishman down under and a rock that supposedly turns up in fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said': Pommie (Australian slang for an English person) plus granite, spoken quickly, sounds like the fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A round red-skinned fruit packed with juicy seeds, a straightforward example of the class.

clue.text: Superior batsman has his eye in?

indicators.note: the words 'Superior batsman' have the eye contained in them, so has signals letters held inside

explanation.surface: A cricketing remark that a top batsman is well set and seeing the ball clearly.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman who 'has his eye in' is settled and judging the ball well; here the eye sits across 'superiOR Batsman'.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary word for an eyeball, the round globe of the organ of sight.

clue.text: Unimaginably high and not fully dressed

definitions.meaning: so tall the summit cannot be seen

explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: towering beyond sight (Marlowe's famous phrase about Troy) and wearing nothing on the upper body.

clue.text: Approving calling for action likely to bring retaliation

parts.note: pro means in favour of
a vocation is a calling

explanation.surface: Supporting a call to arms might provoke a response.
explanation.definitionFit: Deliberate goading that stirs someone to hit back.

clue.text: Chap got on, given guidance

parts.note: a chap is a man
to get on is to grow older, so got on means aged

explanation.surface: A man advanced in some way after being given direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Run or directed by someone, as a business is said to be supervised and steered.

clue.text: Perhaps foot modest Christmas bill for this?

definitions.meaning: a foot, whimsically, is something that occupies a sock
a cheap little present, so a small festive outlay

explanation.surface: Someone may have to pay a small festive bill for a cheap gift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foot' reads as the verb 'pay', but is the body part that occupies a sock.
explanation.definitionFit: A small inexpensive present put into the sock children hang up on Christmas Eve, and whimsically a foot.

clue.text: Odd, unlike MPs arriving to vote?

definitions.meaning: lacking a matching partner, as an odd sock
MPs who agree to abstain together are paired, so one who turns up to vote has no partner

explanation.walkthrough: In the UK Parliament, MPs from opposing sides can 'pair' so both miss a vote without changing the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Without a partner or matching counterpart, like a sock left over after the wash.

clue.text: Victims of war suffered when power station fails

definitions.meaning: the young men killed in the First World War, or the disillusioned survivors
when a plant breaks down, electrical output is gone

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the generation decimated by the Great War, and literally describes output that is gone when a plant breaks down.

clue.text: One on coach perhaps runs into lorry

indicators.note: into means the runs letter goes inside the lorry word

parts.note: a tipper is a lorry with a tilting body for dumping loads
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Someone on a coach crashes into a lorry.
explanation.definitionFit: A day tourist, often travelling on an outing by coach.

clue.text: In a line, start to manoeuvre our defensive resources

indicators.note: In means the following pieces sit inside the line

parts.note: RY is the abbreviation for railway, a line

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Troops in a line begin to manoeuvre our defences.
explanation.definitionFit: A store of weapons, the stockpile a nation relies on for protection.

clue.text: A coup, getting school place first

indicators.note: first says the place word is put at the front, ahead of the school abbreviation

parts.note: to put is to place

explanation.surface: A school wins a coup by getting first place.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden violent seizure of government, a German word for a takeover.

clue.text: Skull with front modified, something dangerously unstable

indicators.note: the front letter of the skull word is changed for another letter

parts.note: the cranium is the skull

explanation.surface: A skull with a damaged forehead suggests something dangerously shaky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with front modified' swaps the C of CRANIUM for U.
explanation.definitionFit: A radioactive heavy metal whose nuclei decay, so it is literally unstable and hazardous.

clue.text: Amateurs having no energy to move round island

indicators.note: moving the letters round rearranges them
having no means one letter is taken out of the word

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Amateurs, out of steam, move around an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having no' removes E from AMATEURS, leaving AMATURS, and 'to move round' rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A large landmass in the Indonesian archipelago, west of Borneo.

clue.text: Slide and almost lose control of car

indicators.note: almost means the last letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: a car that loses grip on the road skids

explanation.surface: A car slides and the driver nearly loses control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the final D from SKID.
explanation.definitionFit: To glide over snow on runners, a kind of sliding.

clue.text: Note enclosed in a pullover exchanged for jumper

indicators.note: enclosed in means the note goes inside the rearranged letters
something exchanged is swapped around, so these letters are reordered

parts.note: te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A note tucked into a sweater that was swapped for another knitted top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exchanged' rearranges 'a pullover' to POLEVAULR, and 'enclosed in' puts the note inside. 'jumper' looks like another sweater, but means an athlete.
explanation.definitionFit: An athlete who leaps over a high bar using a pole is a kind of jumper.

clue.text: Grass up: right conduct for Confucius

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: oat is a cereal grass

explanation.surface: An informer grasses on someone, a Confucian question of right conduct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass up' looks like British slang for informing on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: In Chinese philosophy, the Way, the path of virtue that Confucius taught.

clue.text: For Diana, for example, hard to remove hair braid?

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
to untress is to unbind tresses, loosening plaited hair

explanation.surface: Someone asks if it is hard work for Princess Diana to undo her plait.
explanation.walkthrough: Diana here is the Roman goddess of the chase, not the princess the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman goddess was patron of the chase, the archetypal female hunter.

clue.text: It is surprising I promise to give this

definitions.meaning: one gives one's pledge when promising

explanation.definitionFit: Both an exclamation of astonishment and, literally, the pledge someone hands over when making a promise.
